The ESR treatment was completed November 15, 2002. June 13, 2003 the site was inspected and checked for any establishment of seed coming. The site was again checked August 2003 for any success of the seeding. Seed establishment was spotty and sparse. Vast bare areas were prominent throughout, with massive invasion of Halogeton. An assessment was made September 2003 to determine the problem. It was felt by the team that drought along with a major wind event last spring had contributed to the failure of this project.

During August 2004 the re-drilled rows provided many crested wheatgrass seedlings. However,
the halogeton was thick and 6 to 10 inches tall. There is a hope that the grass will remain and
the annual invasive plants will lose out. This area received a good rain during August 2004.

“I visited the Ibapah ES&R R029 project on August 19, 2004. The ground was
wet as a nice rain occurred there August 18, 2004. The appearance of this
project today is a much different than it was last year (this was formerly a
sagebrush steppe vegetation type). There was little vegetational cover last year
because of the drought. There was much bare ground on the sandy hills leaving
one with the idea that this area was an area of sand dunes. In contract, today,
because of all the moisture, the vegetational ground cover is approximately
60%. However, most of the vegetation is halogeton which shows a lot of vigor
and is 4 to 8 inches tall. Surprisingly, there was only a small amount of
cheatgrass on the site. I visited the Nevada side and there was more cheatgrass
and less halogeton there than on the Utah side.
The first year’s drill rows did not have any seeded plant material in them.
However, the drill rows for FY 2004 had young wheatgrass plants that were 2 to
6 inches apart down each drill row. These young plants were very slender and
were 3 to 6 inches tall. Most of the seeded plants growing are thought to be
Siberian wheatgrass. Due to the wetness of the area, it is felt that these young
plants will get though the rest of the summer, even if it does not rain more this
summer. Since the grasses are cool season and halogeton is mostly a hot season
plant, it is projected that the seeded grasses will do well on this project despite
the halogeton. It was of interest that perhaps halogeton has a slight edge over
Russian thistle for phenological growth behavior. Listed are plants that I
observed. The project needs to be monitored the next two years to fully assess the response
of the seeded bunchgrasses.”

   Goals and general objectives of the project are to:

  B.  Maintain the soil surface factor at the present level by maximizing soil surface cover in the shortest possible timeframe.
  C.  Establish a plant community that would, over the long-term, provide for the diverse needs of the soil an wildlife resources, as well as for domestic livestock.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
The proposed action is needed to minimize the adverse affects of fire to soil, vegetation and wildlife.  Rapid reestablishment of perennial vegetation would reduce soil loss, thus preserving long-term productivity of the area.
   Goals and general objectives of the project are to:
   A.  Reestablish perennial vegetation communities which have a fire resistant characteristics and reduce the opportunity for invasion of undesirable annuals.  Annual vegetation, if allowed to invade these sites, would continue or increase the occurrence of major fires on these areas.
  B.  Maintain the soil surface factor at the present level by maximizing soil surface cover in the shortest possible timeframe.
  C.  Establish a plant community that would, over the long-term, provide for the diverse needs of the soil an wildlife resources, as well as for domestic livestock.

Objectives: The primary objective of the treatment is to seed areas of the burn that are at high risk for significant erosion and non-native species invasion. \r\nEstablish three seeded plants per square meter rooted firmly in soil with consideration for site selection factors of soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and potential for seedling establishment.  Reduce bare ground within the burned area to decrease chance of cheatgrass establishment and lower risk of invasive exotic species gaining dominance.  Protect soil by reducing amount of wind and water erosion.  Provide forage and cover for wildlife and BLM Special Status Species/migratory birds, including crucial winter habitat for mule deer, and sage grouse habitat.
Planned_Implementation: Drill seed approximately 782 acres with a mixture of \u201cHycrest\u201d Crested Wheatgrass, \u201cBannock\u201d Thickspike Wheatgrass, \u201cSecar\u201d Snake River Wheatgrass, \u201cBozoisky\u201d Russian Wildrye, \u201cRimrock\u201d Indian Ricegrass, and \u201cLadak\u201d Alfalfa.  \r\n\r\nDrill seeding 188 acres of a seed mix of native and nonnative species on moderate to high vegetation mortality and moderate burn severity areas to maintain ecological stability, minimize invasion of cheatgrass and noxious weeds and stabilize areas identified as having high wind erosion hazard in order to minimize topsoil loss and fugitive dust.  One seed mix composed of Crested wheatgrass, Russian wildrye, Indian ricegrass, Secar Snake River wheatgrass, Thickspike wheatgrass and alfalfa is proposed.  Range sites within these fires have been analyzed and prioritized for treatment to prevent site degradation, maintain ecological stability, and prevent the spread of non-native, invasive weeds on sites that are suitable for ground seeding methods.  Seeding would utilize species that are adapted to the sites.  Seeding would help quickly establish vegetation that will stabilize soils, reduce erosion, improve soil infiltration of moisture, provide competition for invasive nonnative species and replace organic litter that was consumed by fire.  It is expected that perennial native and non-native grasses, shrubs and forbs will establish within the burned area during the first growing season.  Seeding would be completed using a rangeland drill ahead of or concurrent with fall or winter moisture.  Literature, research, implementation of previous ES and BAR plans, and personal knowledge of BAER team members and Elko Field Office staff has shown success with this timing and application method.  It is expected that vegetation establishment would be successful on all sites although the presence or absence of timely moisture could be a limiting factor.  See Vegetation Treatments - Seeding Map, Appendix IV for proposed ES Plan treatment locations.
Actual_Implementation: Due to the high risk of non-native species invasion coupled with moderate annual precipitation (8-10 inches), a seed mix consisting of both native and non-native species (Russian wildrye, Crested wheatgrass, Bluebunch wheatgrass, Indian ricegrass, Snake River wheatgrass and Alfalfa) was selected.\r\n\r\nThe area received cultural clearance by BLM archeologists prior to treatment implementation. Drilling was done in-house using BLM personnel and either BLM equipment or rented equipment.  Drill seeding continued as ground conditions allowed.  Drill seeding was monitored to ensure that disks were cutting into the soil.  A project inspector was present throughout the process to ensure the treatment met contract specifications.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
BLM monitoring personnel assess the seeding areas yearly to evaluate treatment success.  Effectiveness is based on establishment of three seeded plants per square meter rooted firmly in the soil with consideration to site selection factors such as soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and the potential for seedling establishment. Monitoring data is shared with range staff to provide comparisons with unburned reference sites.

The Mudd Range Drill Seeding was monitored at one location (MUDR – 01) with a permanent modified Freqdens transect. 
Monitoring Results:
2007 – Total seeded species exceed the target density of three plants per square meter, with Alfalfa and Crested Wheatgrass making the greatest contribution. 
2008 – Total seeded species appeared to decline to under one and one-half plants per square meter during the second monitoring year.  Because this monitoring site was read with a permanent transect, we may have more confidence in changes in species numbers from year to year than with plots read with paced transects.  Alfalfa declined precipitously from over two plants per square meter to low density.  Crested Wheatgrass declined and Snake River Wheatgrass more than doubled in density. 
2009 – Crested Wheatgrass continued to decline: it was not recorded during the final monitoring year.  Snake River wheatgrass increased.  Thickspike Wheatgrass was recorded for the first time.  Seeded species seemed well established despite not achieving the target density of three plants per square meter.  The Mudd Range Drill seeding is partially successful.

Objectives: 1. Vegetative cover on this site was primarily Wyoming big sagebrush with little or no understory. Fire impacts have resulted in complete denuding of the landscape. Drill seeding of 800 acres is proposed. Drill seeding is precluded in spring due to nesting upland game concerns. Species selected in the seed mix are intended to be fast rooting for stabilization and limit the establishment and spread of new fire starts in an attempt to break the frequent fire cycle impacting the rest of the burned area while maintaining species diversity found on site pre-fire. Archaeological surveys need to be conducted prior to any drill seeding. Cultural clearances need to be obtained for water haul sites for non-excluded portions of the Plumas Station, Antelope Mountain, and Hallelujah Junction allotments.\r\n2. Vegetative cover needs to be re-established to provide soil stability and to limit gully formation and sedimentation impacting access roads to private residences and prevent undue erosion from the site. Previous drill seeding treatments conducted adjacent to the proposed treatment area in 2007 were observed to be successful. Completion of the proposed action should maintain access to the private residence and limit impacts to Columbia Hill road. After seeding has become established, re-grading and reconditioning of the access roads to the Petersen Mountain Natural Area will be necessary to allow for access from the east and prevent OHV users from creating new roads and trails. Since the site potential is very good and previous seeding actions were successful, the probability of success is high.
Planned_Implementation: Drill seed 800 acres of the burned area with observed soil movement and sedimentation to stabilize soils and prevent closure of access roads to private residences. Drill Seed 710 acres of the burned area with high susceptibility to noxious weed contamination (pepperweed and scotch thistle) to prevent rampant outbreaks of these weed species and keep cheatgrass densities to background values.
Actual_Implementation: ESR Treatments, Red Rock Fire, Drill Seeding was completed, confirmed by GIS attribute table.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results: After driving all accessible roads within the burned area and stopping frequently to check ground conditions, it appeared that on the west side of the burned area thistles and cheatgrass invasion will be a problem in the future. Native bunchgrasses and previously seeded species were found in higher than anticipated quantity, but no new sagebrush regeneration was observed. Unseeded portions of the eastern side of the fire exhibited numerous forbs and thistles and fewer actively growing grasses. Areas seeded with the ES mix appeared to be growing in a \u201cdoghair\u201d manner, which may indicate that seeding in this area was successful. This new growth was especially evident in water collection points, which may indicate that broadcast seed was transported by surface water to the areas especially in need of stabilization.

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
BLM monitoring personnel assess the seeding areas yearly to evaluate treatment success.  Effectiveness is based on establishment of three seeded plants per square meter rooted firmly in the soil with consideration to site selection factors such as soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and the potential for seedling establishment. The Sheep Range Drill Seeding was monitored at one location (SPID – 01) with a permanent modified Freqdens transect. 
Monitoring Results:  
2007 – Seeded species densities varied from very low to relatively high, with Crested Wheatgrass approaching the objective density of three seeded plants per square meter.  Siberian Wheatgrass was indistinguishable from Crested Wheatgrass at the vegetative stage.  Siberian Wheatgrass density may increase (and Crested Wheatgrass density may decrease) as individuals grow easier to distinguish.  Native release appears good but should be regarded skeptically: the main contributor is low-growing Sandberg’s Bluegrass that survived the fire.  Few specimens of Indian Ricegrass were recorded and those were severely drought-stressed.  Moderate amounts of cheatgrass are present at the monitoring site: cheatgrass distribution was patchy. 
2008 – Crested Wheatgrass density increased to almost two and one-half plants per square meter, approaching the objective density of three plants per square meter.  Other seeded species also increased.  
2009 – We may be confident of density figures because this treatment was monitored by a permanent plot.  Crested Wheatgrass declined to under two plants per square meter. Siberian Wheatgrass appeared to increase, but this may be deceptive because Siberian and Crested Wheatgrasses are more difficult to distinguish early in the monitoring period before they have headed out.  Total seeded species density approached so close to the target density we are justified in considering this seeding fully successful.  Native release vegetation only achieved a moderate total density during the final monitoring year.  Sandberg’s Bluegrass declined dramatically.  Apparently, the fire burned very hot at the monitoring location, because few native release grasses were recorded.  The Sandberg’s Bluegrass that was recorded was of very low vigor: it was difficult to distinguish dormant from dead individuals (most specimens displayed the gray foliage typical of dead plants.)  Apparently, many of the Sandberg’s Bluegrass plants that survived the burn died between the 2008 and 2009 monitoring seasons.

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:

The Susie Range Drill Seeding was monitored at one location on the Dry Creek floodplain specifically establish to monitor this seeding (SUDR – 01) with a permanent modified Freqdens transect, and at one location established to monitor the Susie Aerial Wildlife (mule deer) Seeding (SUMD – 01) with a paced density transect.  SUMD – 01 was only monitored during 2009. 

Monitoring Results: 
2007 – Siberian Wheatgrass appeared to be the most successful of seeded species after the first year of growth, approaching a density of two plants per square meter.  Native release was generally sparse at this location, with greatest densities contributed by Green Rabbitbrush. Sandberg’s Bluegrass was not recorded.  
2008 – Seeded species exceeded the objective density of three plants per square meter during the second monitoring season, rendering this seeding already fully successful. Siberian Wheatgrass appeared to fluctuate to a lower density, but this was compensated for by a dramatic increase in Crested Wheatgrass density.  Variable Crested Wheatgrass and Siberian Wheatgrass densities between 2007 and 2008 may be attributable to difficulty distinguishing these species in the field at the vegetative stage of growth.  Total seeded species may be a better measure of success here.  The Big Bluegrass and Snake River Wheatgrass recorded at this location may be present as “orphans” from the Riparian Drill seed mixture which were stuck in the drilling apparatus.  Alternately, the Big Bluegrass present may actually be Nevada Bluegrass (the same species essentially indistinguishable from the cultivar.)  Here these species are considered as native release so their contribution is not overlooked. 
2009 – At SUMD – 01, total seeded species were recorded at a moderate density exceeding one and one-half plant per square meter. At SUDR – 01, seeded species exceeded the objective density of three plants per square meter during the final monitoring season, rendering this seeding fully successful. Objectives: The primary objective is to seed burned areas at high risk for significant erosion and non-native species invasion.  \r\nEstablish three to five seeded plants per square meter rooted firmly in soil with consideration for site selection factors of soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and potential for seedling establishment.   Reduce bare ground within the burn to decrease chance of cheatgrass establishment.  Stabilize the site by protecting the soil and reducing wind and water erosion.  Enhance public safety by reducing driving hazards caused by blowing dust.
Planned_Implementation: Because of these risks coupled with moderate annual precipitation (8-10 inches), a mix of native species was selected.  Seed approximately 20,586 acres with a native drill seed mixture of \u201cSherman\u201d Big Bluegrass, Sandberg\u2019s Bluegrass, \u201cRimrock\u201d Indian Ricegrass, \u201cBannock\u201d Thickspike Wheatgrass, \u201cSecar\u201d Snake River Wheatgrass, and \u201cToe Jam\u201d Bottlebrush Squirreltail. \r\n\r\nDrill seed approximately 21,628 acres of moderate to high vegetation mortality and burn severity in order to maintain ecological stability, minimize invasion of cheatgrass and noxious weeds (bull thistle, hoary cress, and Canada thistle), and stabilize areas identified as having high wind erosion hazard in order to minimize topsoil loss and fugitive dust.  Seed mixes utilize species that are adapted to the sites and are detailed in the specification (part F).  To maximize probability of success, seed will be applied concurrent with fall/winter moisture period between October and December 2006.  First year effectiveness includes stabilization of the soil surface, reducing topsoil loss, improving soil infiltration of moisture, providing competition for invasive non-native species and replacing any organic litter which was consumed by fire.  First season vegetation establishment will be by perennial native and non-native grasses, shrubs and forbs.  It is expected that vegetation establishment will be successful on all sites although the presence or absence of timely moisture could be a limiting factor.  Treatment effectiveness will be monitored (see specification 15).  Specification 12, Cultural Resource Treatment Clearance, has been written to provide for cultural clearance on any ground disturbing activities.  Clearance will be obtained before any treatments proceed.
Actual_Implementation: The area received cultural clearance by BLM archeologists prior to treatment implementation. Drilling was implemented using both BLM personnel (with either BLM equipment or rented equipment) and contracted personnel.  Drill-seeded areas were widely separated.  On some drill-seeded areas \u201cAnatone\u201d Bluebunch Wheatgrass seed was substituted for \u201cSecar\u201d Snake River Wheatgrass seed, and Sandberg\u2019s Bluegrass seed was substituted for \u201cSherman\u201d Big Bluegrass seed.  Exact determination of where modified seed mixtures were applied is not possible.  Seeding proceeded as ground conditions allowed.  Drilling was monitored to ensure disks were cutting into soil. Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
BLM monitoring personnel assess the seeding areas yearly to evaluate treatment success.  Effectiveness is based on establishment of three seeded plants per square meter rooted firmly in the soil with consideration to site selection factors such as soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and the potential for seedling establishment. Monitoring data is shared with range staff to provide comparisons with unburned reference sites.

NOTE: Where monitoring summary refers to "see below&&, refer to the 2009 closeout summary.

The Native Drill Seeding was monitored using permanent modified Freqdens transects at eight separate locations widely distributed across the burn on disjunct drilled areas (monitoring plot WNND – 03 was established on a portion of the Winters burn in the Winnemucca District where these Native Drill seedings were implemented, and is not evaluated here.)  Density numbers may suggest whether the original or modified seed mixtures were applied at any specific monitoring location, but all species applied during the implementation are listed for every monitoring plot. 

Monitoring Results:
2007 – Success varied from location to location across the widely separated disjunct drill seedings, with the seeded patch monitored at WNND – 01 the least successful (density of 0.07 seeded species per square meter) and WNND – 03 the most successful (density of 7.96 seeded species per square meter.)  It important to note that at these two monitoring points (and in general across all the drill seeding monitoring plots) there appears to be an inverse relationship between the density of preexisting Sandberg’s Bluegrass and the germinating density of total seeded species.  The established community of Sandberg’s Bluegrass at WNND – 01 was recorded at 30.64 plants per square meter: at WNND – 03 Sandberg’s Bluegrass density was recorded at only 1.22.  These numbers constitute evidence that the presence of a dense community of Sandberg’s Bluegrass at any given location scheduled for drill seeding is likely to render that seeding ineffective. 
Density numbers recorded at individual monitoring plot locations are presented above for interpretation, but the large array of densities for all monitoring sites confounds convenient analysis.  Unknown environmental factors (in addition to preexisting Sandberg’s Bluegrass), could have influenced disparate results recorded at different monitoring locations.  For convenience, an amalgamation of some results may be desirable because eight of the nine monitoring locations were established on Loamy 8-10 inch range sites (the most common range site across the large drill-seeded area.)  To encourage a general understanding of drill seeding success on Loamy 8-10 inch range sites across the treated area, density numbers for all seeded species (only) at all monitoring locations, are averaged below.  
Total average densities for seeded species on drilled areas of Loamy 8-10 inch range sites indicate that “on average,” the drill seeding was approaching the lower end of the objective density of three plants per square meter after the first year of growth.  This average should be interpreted very cautiously, especially with regard to results for Snake River Wheatgrass and Bluebunch Wheatgrass; and for results for Big Bluegrass and seeded Sandberg’s Bluegrass, since these species were substituted for each other on indeterminate seeded patches.  
The ninth monitoring plot for the Winters burn Native Drill Seeding (WNND – 10) was established on a Sandy 8-10 inch range site, so comparisons with other results are less useful.  On the sandy site, seeded species had exceeded the objective density of three to five plants per square meter by the end of the first monitoring season, with Indian Ricegrass making the greatest contribution.   The Crested Wheatgrass and Russian Wildrye recorded at WNND – 07 during the second and final monitoring years are probably “orphans” stuck in the drilling apparatus and unintentionally introduced into the site. 

2008 – On the sandy site seeded species continued to exceed the objective density of three to five plants per square meter by the end of the second monitoring season, with Thickspike Wheatgrass making the greatest contribution.  The trade-off of Indian Ricegrass for Thickspike Wheatgrass, which appeared to occur between the first and second year of monitoring is perplexing.  It is possible the Indian Ricegrass seedlings recorded the first year failed to establish and were replaced by slow-starting Thickspike Wheatgrass seedlings during the second year.  Misidentifications are unlikely because the same technician read the plots both years, and seedlings of these species are easy to differentiate.  Average densities for all Native Drill Seeding monitoring plots are presented below. 
Total average densities for seeded species on drilled areas of Loamy 8-10 inch range sites indicate that “on average,” the drill seeding remained relatively constant, still approaching the lower end of the objective density of three plants per square meter after the second year of growth.  

2009 – Average densities for all Native Drill Seeding monitoring plots are presented below. 
Total average densities for seeded species on drilled areas of Loamy 8-10 inch range sites indicate that “on average,” the drill seeding doubled in density the final year of monitoring, well exceeding the target density for total seeded species.  The numerous disjunct patches composing the Winters Native Drill Seeding are marked by subtle differences in environmental factors of soils, topography, and grazing history.  Under such divergent conditions, the drill seeding responded slightly differently over the three growing seasons on each seeded area. 
The Native Drill Seeding also exceeded the target density where it was applied on the Sandy 8-10 inch range site (WNND – 10). 
The native drill seed mixture included numerous species, including commonly seeded Big Bluegrass, Indian Ricegrass, Thickspike Wheatgrass, Snake River Wheatgrass, and rarely seeded Sandberg’s Bluegrass and Bottlebrush Squirreltail.  Success of each seeded species varied on disjunct patches with environmental conditions.  The large number of species applied appears to have provided a built-in flexibility to the response of the mixture to variation of environmental conditions across treated areas.  Thickspike Wheatgrass and Indian Ricegrass were most successful on the sandy site.  Bluebunch Wheatgrass and Snake River Wheatgrass were most successful on loamy sites that may have been in better range condition prior to the burn.  The rarely seeded Sandberg’s Bluegrass and Bottlebrush Squirreltail were most successful on clayey sites that may have been in poorer range condition prior to the burn. 
The Winters Native Drill seeding was fully successful across wide areas, probably attributable to the numerous species with unique ecological tolerances that made up the seed mixture.

Objectives: To limit the long term establishment of cheatgrass within the burn area through the establishment of a perennial plant community on 70-80% of the crested wheatgrass seeding area.
Planned_Implementation:
The area chosen for treatment consists of the 900 acres to be drill seeded as well as the southern portion of the fire, which is predominately native vegetation. The seeded area may be closed to livestock grazing for at least two years.

Approximately 900 acres would be drill seeded with crested wheatgrass at lbs/acre. The treatment would occur predominantly within the North Brush Pasture (north end of the fuel).
The proposed treatment area is currently a crested wheatgrass seeding (although there are large areas dominated by cheatgrass found throughout it) within a 7-9 inch precipitation
zone. Prior to any drill seeding activities, a cultural survey would need to be conducted. This would be accomplished through a cultural clearance contract. In addition the seeded
area may be closed to livestock grazing for at least 2 years following treatment.
Actual_Implementation:
The aerial application of herbicide to target cheatgrass was slated to occur in the fall of 2017 followed by the ground seeding of Siberian wheatgrass in the fall of 2018. The aerial application of herbicides was postponed due to a concern about potential drift onto nearby agricultural lands due to the lack of vegetative cover within the burned area. Therefore, the drill seeding of Siberian wheatgrass was completed in the fall of 2017 to help establish a vegetative cover prior to the aerial application of herbicides. The aerial application of herbicide in 2018 did not occur due to a lack of
funding.
Approximately 1,000 acres were ground seeded with a mixture of
Ladak alfalfa, Vavilov I Siberian wheatgrass, Vavilov II Siberian
wheatgrass, Anatone bluebunch wheatgrass, and Sherman big
bluegrass at approximately 13 lbs/acre. Tractor was rented on Sept
22, 2017. Archeological clearances were conducted by the PFO
archeologist and PFO employees from Oct 3rd-5th, 2017. Cadastral
survey markers were located and protected on Oct 12th, 2017. Drill
seeding was completed from Oct 16th –Nov 1st, 2017.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
In 2019, all monitoring sites established in 2017 were re-sampled. An additional four plots were established just outside the burn perimeter to determine the difference between unburned areas, drill seeded areas and burned, non-drill seeded areas. The four plots established outside the burn perimeter show that annual grass canopy cover was extensive at 98% canopy cover with low perennial grass canopy cover (approx. 10%). Within the drill seeded treatment area, the canopy cover of non-native perennial grasses has achieved the objective of 70-80% canopy cover of non-native perennial grasses. Cheatgrass continues to exist within the treated area as patches compared to almost complete dominance outside of the fire perimeter.
The area chosen for drill seeding was selected due to a decrease of deep-rooted perennial grasses, either native or non-native, compared to other areas within the fire perimeter that were not chosen for treatment.  The seeded portion of the fire received two years of rest prior to utilization in 2020.  However, due to the utilization prior to monitoring direct comparison of percent foliar cover between 2018, 2019, and 2020 is not possible nor is determining if objectives were met. 
Based on the foliar cover data collected in 2018 and 2019 and the basal cover data collected in 2020, it appears that there was an increase in crested wheatgrass/Siberian wheatgrass, and bluebunch wheatgrass within the drill seeded area.  Between 2018 and 2019 there was a 171% increase in percent cover of non-native perennial species within the treated area compared to an 13% increase in the untreated area within the fire perimeter.  There appears to be little difference in the percent cover of either Sandburg bluegrass or cheatgrass for drill seeded areas vs non-drill seeded areas within the fire perimeter. 
The presence of perennial grasses, both native and non-native, appear to be reducing the percent cover of cheatgrass compared to control plots established immediately adjacent to the fire perimeter.  Within the fire perimeter, average percent cover of cheatgrass (seeded and non-seeded areas combined) was 41% compared to 74% for the control plots in 2020. 

2018: At the
time monitoring occurred in 2018, small plants (approximately 1 inch in diameter) had
established in drill rows within the treated area. The initial results indicate that crested
wheatgrass/Siberian Wheatgrass canopy cover was greater within the seeded portion of the
burned area than in those areas not drill seeded. Cheatgrass and Sandberg bluegrass cover was
nearly identical both within and outside of the drill seeding treatment area. It is expected that as
the newly establish Siberian wheatgrass plants grow they will be better able to complete with
cheatgrass. This should decrease the percent canopy cover of the annual grass.

2019 Monitoring
Two AIM plots were monitored in the Cobble Complex ESR on July 1, and July 12, 2019.
Density and perennial frequency were measured using .4 meter quadrats (0.16 M2) in a belt
transect. The perennial species that have been establishing up to this point is impressive, with the
total perennial frequency averaging 92%. The perennial relative frequency is on track to meet the
targeted 30%, with an average of 24% in 2019. The precipitation this year was slightly above
normal. Into the second growing season there was an increase in foliar cover, with an average of
88%, although much of the foliar cover consisted of invasive species with an average of 68%
being Cheatgrass. The density of seeded and perennial species averaged 19 plants per square
meter, above the seedling objective of 4 plants per square meter. The weeds crew visited the site
in July and the area was not treated because no noxious weeds were found. 
PART 9-RECOMMENDATIONS/CONCLUSIONS
The ESR drill seeding treatment on the Cobble Complex Fire shows good results into the second
season following the fire. New seedlings are getting established and the relative frequency of
perennial vegetation is nearly meeting the 30% frequency objective. The photos included in this
report show how the area is now much more dense in vegetation with taller perennial grasses,
although much of the lower cover is cheatgrass. Invasives are present in large numbers and
increased since last year, seeded and re-established desirable perennials species should be
competitive into the third growing season.
The ESR protection fence was constructed and completed in 2018. AIM protocols for Soil
Stability were not conducted in the 1st year following the fire, due to extreme soil instability that
is typical the first year after a burn. Soil Stability will be collected in October 2019.

2018 - The ESR drill seeding treatment on the Cobble Complex Fire shows good results the first
growing season following the fire. New seedlings are getting established and frequency of
perennial vegetation is on track to meet the 30% frequency objective within 3 years. Although
invasives are present in large numbers, seeded and re-established desirable perennials species
should be competitive into the second growing season with enough precipitation. Precipitation
in this area was about one-third of normal during the 2018 water year. Given the low
precipitation at the Cobble Complex site and the continuous stand of cheatgrass that was present
before these fires, a strong-establishing seed mix was developed for these drill seeding
treatments. Given the prevalence of cheatgrass and below-average ppt. at a site that is already a
historically dry site, the seeding results up to this point are impressive.

2019 - In the second growing season after the Dutch Mt. fire in 2017, the site was fully successful in

frequency was 94%, and much of that success was due to re-established perennials. Perennial
relative frequency/composition this year was 56.3%, surpassing the 30% relative frequency
objective, with an increase of seeded species by 19.5% when compared to last year’s seeded

PART 9 – RECOMMENDATIONS/CONCLUSIONS
The Rabbit Creek fire will continue to have residual effects across the landscape for many years, but the planning, treatments, and monitoring accomplished in the last year have provided a steppingstone to continue with the restoration efforts throughout the burn area. One of the biggest lessons learned is that restoration takes time when you are dealing with environmental effects. There are many factors that go into restoring burn areas, some are human, but many are environmental. Goals and objectives will continue to be developed for restoring the Rabbit Creek Fire and the lessons learned from this fire will be used for future planning in Emergency Stabilization and Rehabilitation.

The Copper Fire will be reseeded with a drill seeder. Any changes to seed mix will take into

unburned islands, and any identified historic properties. Seeding will occur in the fall, winter,

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Density Results:
2021: The rehab objective for the aerial seeding of 1 native forb/m2 and 3 seeded grasses/m2 along with the drill seeding objective of 3 seeded species/m2 were not fully met. Seeded grass species nearly met the goal at 2.42/m2 with Indian ricegrass being the most dominant grass species across the plots. Cover
2021: Average foliar cover was extremely low across the 9 plots at 0.59% average. Shafter 02A had the highest percentage of foliar cover at 1.33% while 4 of the plots observed 0.00% foliar cover. During Line-Point Intercept the only identified species was Longleaf phlox (Phlox longifolia) and it was observed only once, accounting for the 0.07% perennial forbs cover. The other 8 total hits were species that were identified as either “Unknown” or “Dead Beyond Recognition”.
Gaps and Erosion
2021: Given the extremely low foliar cover it is appropriate that the most frequently observed gap size class was >200cm at 99.41%. No data was collected about signs of erosion on the plot but it stands to reason that these plots are very vulnerable to wind and water erosion while the coverage and therefore stabilizing root systems are essentially non-existent across the plots.

Recommendations:
2021: The ESR rehabilitation objectives od the drill/aerial sage seedings have not been fully met. It is strongly recommended that the closure of the Collar and Elbow pastures should remain in place in order to allow the area to receive proper rest so that seeded species may have the opportunity to establish root systems on site.

ESR 2022 Monitoring Report
S2 Drill Seeding/S3 Aerial Sage Seeding
Shafter Complex AIM Plots 01, 01A, 01B, 02, 02A, 02B, 03, 03A, and 03B are located in a Rangeland Loamy 12-16” P.Z. site in a former Artemisia tridentata ssp. vaseyana (Mountain big sagebrush), Symphoricarpos oreophilus (Mountain snowberry), Amelanchier utahensis (Utah serviceberry), Purshia tridentata (Antelope bitterbrush), Pseudoroegneria spicata (Bluebunch wheatgrass), Achnatherum thurberianum (Thurber’s needlegrass), and Achnatherum occidentale (Western needlegrass) vegetation community on concave mountain side slopes.
All these plots were treated with Drill and Aerial seeding mixes which consisted of Russian wildrye (Psathyrostachys juncea), Siberian wheatgrass (Agropyron fragile), Snake River wheatgrass (Elymus wawawaiensis), Indian ricegrass (Achnatherum hymenoides), Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda), Blue flax (Linum perenne), Black sagebrush (Artemisia nova), Wyoming big sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata ssp. wyomingensis), and Western yarrow (Achillea millefolium).

Density Results
2021: The rehab objective for the aerial seeding of 1 native forb/m2 and 3 seeded grasses/m2 along with the drill seeding objective of 3 seeded species/m2 were not fully met. Seeded grass species nearly met the goal at 2.42/m2 with Indian ricegrass being the most dominant grass species across the plots. Native regrowth of forbs was dominated by Phlox species but was still not dense enough to meet the objective at just 0.45 native forbs/m2. No seeded species were observed, in fact all but one shrub observed in the density plots were identified as “Dead Beyond Recognition”.
2022: The rehabilitation objectives as stated above have not been met. Seeded grasses were less abundant than in 2021, moving further away from achieving the objective. Native regrowth of perennial grasses increased slightly but regrowth of forbs and shrubs declined.
AIM Data Results
Cover
2021: Average foliar cover was extremely low across the 9 plots at 0.59% average. Shafter 02A had the highest percentage of foliar cover at 1.33% while 4 of the plots observed 0.00% foliar cover. During Line-Point Intercept the only identified species was Longleaf phlox (Phlox longifolia) and it was observed only once, accounting for the 0.07% perennial forbs cover. The other 8 total hits were species that were identified as either “Unknown” or “Dead Beyond Recognition”.
2022: Average foliar cover increased but was still very low across the plots at 10.4%. Annual forbs increased most significantly and are now the most dominant on the plot at 5.4% followed by perennial grasses at 3.6% total. The increase of foliar cover is good for stabilizing the soil but this situation is still prime for an annual forb or annual grass invasion and takeover so this treatment will need continued monitoring to determine if any future treatments will be necessary.
Gaps and Erosion
2021: Given the extremely low foliar cover it is appropriate that the most frequently observed gap size class was >200cm at 99.41%. No data was collected about signs of erosion on the plot but it stands to reason that these plots are very vulnerable to wind and water erosion while the coverage and therefore stabilizing root systems are essentially non-existent across the plots.
2022: Gaps were still extremely dominant on these plots but with the slight increase in foliar cover there was a slight redistribution of gaps from the larger size ranges to the smaller ranges. Knowing the foliar makeup of the plots it will be important to make sure that the reduction of gaps is due to an increase in perennial cover and not annual cover. Plots 03B and 02 had the most soil erosion and disturbance observed with gullies and waterflow patterns noted.
Species Richness
2021: Average total species count was low at 9. Perennials did outnumber annuals and the presence of shrubs and trees show signs of potential for site rehabilitation in the future.
2022: Average total species count was moderate and increased by 15 species identified. Many of the new species identified were annual forbs, 8 added species, but perennial forbs and perennial grasses increased by 3 species each. The number of perennial species observed on the plot could indicate potential future success but remained threatened by the high number of annuals present.
Recommendations:
2021: The ESR rehabilitation objectives of the drill/aerial sage seedings have not been fully met. It is strongly recommended that the closure of the Collar and Elbow pastures should remain in place in order to allow the area to receive proper rest so that seeded species may have the opportunity to establish root systems on site.
2022: The ESR rehabilitation objective of the drill/aerial sage seeding have not been fully met. It is strongly recommended that the closure of the Collar and Elbow pastures should remain in place in order to allow the area to receive proper rest so that seeded species may have the opportunity to establish root systems on site. The increase of foliar cover can help the soil stabilize but continued monitoring and possibly additional treatment should be continued in the future.
PART 9 – RECOMMENDATIONS/CONCLUSIONS
The Shafter Complex Fire will continue to have residual effects across the landscape for many years, but the planning, treatments and monitoring accomplished in the last year have provided a steppingstone to continue with the restoration efforts throughout the burn area. One of the biggest lessons learned is that restoration takes time when you are dealing with environmental effects. There are many factors that go into restoring burn areas, some are human but many are environmental. Goals and objectives will continue to be developed for restoring the Shafter Complex Fire and the lessons learned from this fire will be used for future planning in Emergency Stabilization and Rehabilitation.

FY2021 received more winter and spring precipitation (Nov. 2020 – May 2021) than the
same time period in FY2020, which could have influenced the spike in perennial growth and/or
vigor illustrated by the percent perennial cover. All three transects of Plot T130-UpperQuinn-
RBL-20 had high percent perennial cover; transect one 42% perennial cover, while transects two
and three both had 44% perennial cover (averaging 43% for the plot).
Additionally, site T130-UpperQuinn-RBL-20 saw an increase in plant species diversity
between 2020 and 2021. In 2020, it was noted that the density of 4 plants/sq. meter was entirely
AGFR. In 2021 however, while the average density was again 4 plants/sq. meter, seeded species
recorded included PSSP6, AGCR, AGFR, and POSE. AGCR was the dominant species, with 62
individuals being recorded, followed by PSSP6 and AGFR with 31 and 25 individuals
respectively, while POSE only had 1 individual recorded.
The increase in percent perennial cover from 2020 to 2021 compared to the stagnant
density in 2020 and 2021 suggests that there was increase in shrub cover (basal and/or canopy)
and/or an overall increase in perennial vigor resulting in larger individuals.

Monitoring Conclusions
FY2022 received somewhat higher precipitation (Oct. 2021 – Sept. 2022) than the same time period in FY2020, which could have influenced the spike in perennial growth and/or vigor illustrated by the percent perennial cover for one of the three plots. The only plot, South Lewallen 01, had a high percent perennial cover and meet/over exceeded its ESR objective (54.7%).
The other two plots, T130-UpperQuinn-RBL-20 and South Lewallen 02, had dips in their percent perennial cover and did not meet their ESR objective. T130-UpperQuinn-RBL-20 had a 12% and South Lewallen had a 17.3% percent perennial cover, respectively 31% and 13.7% lower than the FY 2021 percent perennial cover results. As for density, T130-UpperQuinn-RBL-20 is not meeting the ESR objective of 3 plants/sq. meter. Last year, FY 2021, there was 4 plants/sq. meter but for this year FY 2022 had 1.9 plants/sq. meter. However, South Lewallen 01 had 14.5 plants/sq. meter much higher than FY 2021 results of 2 plants/sq meter and over exceeded the ESR objective of 3 plants/sq. meter. As for South Lewallen 02, density was not monitored for FY 2022.
One major takeaway in the Monitoring Results Summary section is that Sandberg bluegrass and Wyoming big sagebrush was a seeded species that was seen at two of the three sites besides the third site having Siberian wheatgrass and basin wildrye.
